mcq.q: The model proposes refund(order_id, amount). What decides the amount?
options: The model, from what it read in the order
Deterministic code from the order record and policy
The amount the user asks for in the message
The refund rules written into the prompt
mcq.why: The model proposes; code computes amounts and enforces limits.
distractors: The model proposes; it must not compute money.
Users can ask for anything; the record and policy decide.

mcq.q: Where should a tenant ID for a tool call come from?
options: The tenant ID in the model's call arguments
The authenticated session
The retrieved document
The tenant named in the system prompt text
mcq.why: Identity and tenant come from trusted context, never from model output.
distractors: The model can be wrong or manipulated; never trust it for identity.
A retrieved document is data, and could even be planted.
Prompts are not an authorisation mechanism.

mcq.q: What is the core pattern for combining a model with business rules?
options: The model interprets and proposes; code validates, decides, executes
Rules are written into the prompt, which the model follows exactly
The model decides everything, and code just records the result
Code only formats the output after the model has decided
mcq.why: Rules must be exact, auditable and identical every time.
distractors: Prompted rules are probabilistic, not exact.
Decisions with exact rules belong in code.
Code must validate and decide, not just format.

mcq.q: Which jobs suit the model?
options: Enforcing permissions on every tool call
Intent, field extraction, wording, ranking
Choosing the next workflow state transition
Computing refund amounts from the policy
mcq.why: Fuzzy tasks go to the model; exact ones to code.
distractors: State transitions must be deterministic: code.

mcq.q: Which jobs belong in code?
options: Drafting a friendly reply to the customer
Amounts, limits, permissions, state, legal text
Ranking search results by their relevance
Understanding what a free-text request means
mcq.why: These must be exact and auditable.
distractors: Wording is fuzzy work the model does well.
Understanding intent is the model's job.

mcq.q: A prompt says “apply a 10% discount for customers over 2 years, max $500”. In production some customers get 15%. What is the fix?
options: Move the rule into code; the model only extracts the request
Make the prompt longer, spelling out every edge case
Add “please be careful with discounts” to the prompt
Use a higher temperature so the outputs vary less
mcq.why: Exact, testable and auditable behaviour needs code.
distractors: More words still leave the rule probabilistic.
Pleading does not make sampling exact.
Higher temperature makes outputs vary more.

mcq.q: The model replies “done” but the database write failed. What should the system report?
options: Nothing
Whatever the model said
The actual result of the write
Success, to keep the user happy
mcq.why: Never report success from model text.
distractors: The model does not know whether the write succeeded.

mcq.q: What should the boundary between model and rules look like?
options: Hidden inside the prompt, so the model applies it
Free text passed straight to the database
Decided by the user each time they ask
A typed proposal that code accepts or rejects, logging why
mcq.why: Explicit boundaries make behaviour auditable.
distractors: A prompt is not an enforceable boundary.
Free text cannot be validated reliably.
Users cannot be the authority on rules.

mcq.q: The model extracts “2 seats” when the account has 5. What catches it?
options: Checking against the account record
The model's own confidence score
A longer, more detailed prompt
Nothing; extraction errors are unavoidable
mcq.why: Check extracted values against systems of record.

mcq.q: Which tool guarantees that a local model's output matches a JSON Schema or grammar by masking tokens?
options: Outlines
LiteLLM
DSPy
MLflow Tracking
mcq.why: Instructor, by contrast, validates and re-asks on failure.
distractors: LiteLLM is a gateway across providers; it does not mask tokens.
DSPy optimises prompts and pipelines; it does not constrain decoding.

mcq.q: A model-written reply says “Your refund of ₹2,400 has been processed”, but the refund API call failed. Which design rule was broken?
options: The model should have computed the amount more carefully
The prompt should have told the model to be accurate
The temperature was too high for a financial message
Users must see the outcome read from the system, not the model's claim
mcq.why: The model should explain the real result returned by the refund service, which was a failure.
distractors: The amount is not the problem; the action failed.
A prompt cannot make the model know the API's result.
Sampling settings cannot reveal a failed call.

interview.q: Explain the “model proposes, code disposes” pattern.
interview.followUp: Give an example where the model's proposal must be modified, not just accepted or rejected.

interview.q: Which parts of a refund flow belong to the model and which to code?
interview.followUp: The customer disputes the amount. What do you show them, and from where?

interview.q: Why are prompted business rules unreliable?
covers: No audit trail of the rule
interview.followUp: The rule works in every test. Why is that still not enough?

interview.q: A team wants the model to decide discounts from the chat. How do you redesign it?
covers: Rule in code with clear inputs
interview.followUp: How would you show the business owner the rule now behaves exactly as written?

interview.q: How do you make sure users see the true outcome of an action?
covers: Read the result from the system
Never trust model claims of success
interview.followUp: The action partly succeeded. What does the user see?

interview.q: {company}'s assistant explains fee waivers. Design how waivers are actually decided and recorded.
interview.followUp: How would you show an auditor why a specific waiver was granted?

interview.q: Design the boundary between an LLM and a workflow engine for an enterprise assistant.
interview.followUp: How would you test the boundary?

interview.q: {assistant} changes bookings. Design the flow so fees, rules and outcomes are always exact.
covers: Code applies fare rules and computes fees
Supplier call result decides the outcome
interview.followUp: The supplier's fee differs from your computed fee. Which wins, and what does the traveller see?

mcq.q: Which errors are worth retrying?
options: 400 Bad Request, after a short pause
429 and 5xx, with backoff and jitter
Schema validation failures on the output
All errors, immediately and as often as needed
mcq.why: Rate limits and transient server errors can succeed later; a 400 is your bug.
distractors: The request is malformed; retrying repeats the failure.
Retrying may help once, but it is a validation issue, not a transient error.

mcq.q: Which timeouts should an LLM call have?
options: Only a limit on the size of the response body
Connect, total deadline, and an idle timeout for streams
None, since the provider manages its own timeouts
Only a connect timeout on the first request
mcq.why: LLM latency has a long tail; without deadlines, connections pile up.
distractors: Size limits do not bound time.
Without your own timeouts, calls can hang.
A slow response can still hang after connecting.

mcq.q: Backoff waits base × 2^attempt. With a base of 0.5 s, how long is the wait before attempt 3 (counting from 0)?
options: 4 s
2 s
8 s
mcq.why: 0.5 × 2³ = 4 s, then randomised by jitter.
distractors: That uses a base of 1 s.

mcq.q: Why add jitter to retries?
options: To make each retry happen sooner
To reduce the number of attempts allowed
To change the error code the server returns
To spread retries so clients do not spike together
mcq.why: Synchronised retries can knock a recovering service over again.

mcq.q: A provider returns 429 with a Retry-After header. What should the client do?
options: Retry immediately, before others do
Wait at least as long as it asks
Ignore the header and use a fixed delay
Switch off retries for that provider forever
mcq.why: Respect the server's guidance.
distractors: That ignores the server's request and adds load.
The header tells you when capacity returns.

mcq.q: What is a client-side token bucket for?
options: Tracking rate limits, so you queue instead of being rejected
Caching answers to repeated questions to save tokens
Counting the number of active users in each region
Storing the API keys for each provider securely
mcq.why: Providers limit requests and tokens per minute.
distractors: Users are not what the limits count.
Keys belong in a secret store.

mcq.q: Why must fallback models be evaluated too?
options: Their quality and format may differ
They are never used in practice
They are always better than the primary
They need no prompts of their own
mcq.why: A fallback that breaks the format causes new failures.
distractors: Outages make them run in production.
They are often weaker or different.
Prompts may need adapting per model.

mcq.q: Which are token budgets the topic recommends? Choose all that apply.
options: Per-user or per-tenant daily spend
A cap on input tokens
max_tokens on output
Unlimited output for important users
mcq.why: Budgets bound cost and latency.
distractors: Unbounded output is a cost and latency risk.

mcq.q: Retrying without a retry budget or admission control during a slowdown tends to…
options: Fix the slowdown by sending more requests
Reduce the load on the struggling service
Have no effect on the provider's health
Turn a slowdown into an outage
mcq.why: Retries add load exactly when capacity is short.
distractors: More requests add load to a struggling service.

mcq.q: 20% of 2,000 requests per second fail, and each failure is retried up to 3 times. How much extra load can that add?
options: Up to 400
Up to 6,000
Up to 1,200
Up to 600
mcq.why: 400 failures × 3 retries = 1,200 more requests per second at worst.
distractors: That is the failures only, retried once.
That multiplies all requests by 3, not just the failures.
That is three retries for 10% of traffic; 20% of 2,000 is 400 failures, × 3 = 1,200.

interview.q: Which errors are worth retrying, and how?
interview.followUp: A 500 came back from a call that charges money. Do you retry?

interview.q: What timeouts does an LLM call need?
interview.followUp: How would you choose the values for each?

interview.q: Why do retries need jitter?
interview.followUp: How would you pick the jitter range?

interview.q: Design a call wrapper for LLM requests.
interview.followUp: What would you log on every retry?

interview.q: Your provider is rate-limiting you at peak. What do you do?
interview.followUp: The provider will not raise your limits. What next?

interview.q: {company}'s refund call timed out. Should you retry, and how?
covers: Never blindly: it may have succeeded
Query status with an idempotency key
interview.followUp: The status check also times out. What do you do?

interview.followUp: How would you test the fallback before a real outage?

interview.q: {company}'s festival sale starts with provider throttling. Design the client behaviour so retries do not make it worse.
interview.followUp: Which requests would you shed first, and why?

mcq.q: How does the cost shape of a hosted API differ from self-hosting?
options: Hosted: per token, scales to zero. Self-hosted: per GPU-hour, cheap only if busy
Hosted is always cheaper, whatever the volume or utilisation
They cost about the same once a team is running at a large scale
Self-hosted is always cheaper, since there is no per-token fee to pay
mcq.why: Idle GPUs still cost money; hosted APIs charge only for use (14.8).
distractors: At high, steady volume self-hosting can be cheaper.

mcq.q: Which option gives full control over data, including air-gapped operation?
options: Any hosted API with its default settings
Prompt caching on a hosted provider
Public leaderboards for open models
Self-hosting open-weight models
mcq.why: Hosted data control depends on contract, region and retention settings.
distractors: Data control depends on contract, region and retention.
Caching is a cost feature, not data control.
Leaderboards rank models; they host nothing.

mcq.q: Why are public leaderboards a weak basis for choosing a model?
options: They only measure speed and latency, not answer quality
They are private, so their results cannot be checked
General skills on public, possibly contaminated data
They are always wrong about how models really rank
mcq.why: Build a task-specific evaluation set instead.
distractors: They are informative, just not about your task.

mcq.q: How large should a first task-specific evaluation set be, according to the topic?
options: At least 100,000 labelled examples
About 50–200 real examples with outcomes
Only synthetic examples from a model
One example per category is enough
mcq.why: Small enough to build quickly, large enough to compare 3–5 candidates.
distractors: That is far more than a first set needs.
Real examples show your real task.

mcq.q: Model A scores 92% at $0.01 per request; model B 88% at $0.002. The acceptance bar is 85%. Which should you choose?
options: Both equally
Model A
Neither
Model B
mcq.why: Choose the cheapest model that meets the bar; B passes at a fifth of the cost.
distractors: A is better but costs five times more than needed.

mcq.q: What should a model comparison measure together?
options: Quality, latency and cost
Only answer quality, on the test set
Only the cost per million tokens
Only the advertised context length
mcq.why: A model that is accurate but too slow or expensive fails the product.
distractors: A cheap model may fail the task.

mcq.q: 150 tickets are labelled by two people, and the 140 they agree on are kept with a short scoring script. What does this become?
options: Production traffic for the new model
A submission to a public leaderboard
A training set for pretraining a model
Baseline, selection tool and first regression test
mcq.why: Chapter 8 grows it into a full evaluation practice.
distractors: It is a curated test set, not live traffic.

mcq.q: Which is an operational risk specific to hosted APIs?
options: Your own capacity planning and on-call
GPU failures in your own data centre
Outages, rate limits and deprecations
Driver updates on your own servers
mcq.why: Self-hosting swaps these for your own on-call and capacity work.

mcq.q: A team picks a model because it advertises a 1M-token context. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; long context means better answers
An advertised feature is not evidence; test it
Long contexts are always used well by models
Context length alone decides the model's cost
mcq.why: Choose with your own data (5.3, 5.7).
distractors: Advertised length is not evidence of quality.
Middle positions are often used less reliably.
Cost depends on tokens used and price.

mcq.q: When should you re-run your model comparison?
options: Only when the team changes
Never; once is enough
When models or prices change
Only after an outage
mcq.why: New releases and price changes can change the cheapest model that meets the bar (18.5).

mcq.q: Three models pass a ticket task's acceptance bar of 90% accuracy: A scores 96% at $12 per 1,000 tickets, B 92% at $3, and C 90.5% at $1.50 with latency above target. Which should you choose?
options: None: no model reached 100% on the evaluation set
C: it is the cheapest of the three that passes on accuracy
A: it scores highest, so it is the safest choice
B: the cheapest that meets both the quality bar and the latency target
mcq.why: C fails the latency target, and A costs four times B for accuracy the bar does not need.
distractors: It misses the latency target, which is part of the bar.
The rule is the cheapest model that meets the bar, not the best scorer.

interview.followUp: Which would you choose for a pilot, and when would you revisit that choice?

Use as baseline and regression test
interview.followUp: How would you keep the set representative as traffic changes?

interview.q: Your company must keep customer data in-country. How does that change model selection?
covers: Contract and region terms for hosted options
interview.followUp: The best model is only available in another region. What are your options?

interview.q: {company} must choose a model for shopper questions in four languages at festival-peak volume. How would you decide?
covers: A routing mix: mid-size default, frontier for escalation
interview.followUp: Tamil quality is below the bar on every affordable model. What do you do?

interview.followUp: A new model is released mid-quarter. Do you wait?

interview.q: {company} is choosing models for its booking agent. How would you assign models to steps?
interview.followUp: How would you measure cost per completed booking?

mcq.q: Which message roles does a typical chat API use?
options: Query, key and value roles
Admin, guest and bot roles
System, user, assistant, tool
Input and output messages only
mcq.why: System holds the developer's persistent instructions; tool holds results of tool calls.
distractors: Those are attention vectors, not message roles.

mcq.q: Why put the stable parts of a prompt first?
options: It reduces the vocabulary the model uses
Stable parts can be prompt-cached
It is required by the JSON message format
Models ignore the end of long prompts
mcq.why: A stable prefix can be reused across requests (14.3).
distractors: Order does not change the vocabulary.
JSON does not care about order.
The end is often read well; the input goes last.

mcq.q: Why delimit retrieved context clearly, for example with XML-style tags?
options: To speed up decoding of the answer
Because models cannot read plain text
To separate data from instructions, for safety
To make the prompt shorter overall
mcq.why: It helps against instructions hidden in documents (16.2).
distractors: Tags do not make decoding faster.
They can; tags mark what is data.

mcq.q: How many few-shot examples does the topic suggest, and what kind?
options: Exactly one example of the output
50 near-identical examples
None ever, since they confuse models
2–5 diverse pairs with edge cases
mcq.why: Examples are strong signals; diversity stops the model copying surface details.

mcq.q: All your few-shot examples use the same customer name and product. What risk does this create?
options: The prompt becomes invalid and is rejected
The model copies those details into other answers
Nothing, as long as the format is correct
The model refuses to answer other customers
mcq.why: Vary the examples' surface features.
distractors: Examples are strong signals, including details.
It answers, but leaks the details.

mcq.q: How should instructions be written?
options: Only as prohibitions of what not to do
As vague as possible to allow flexibility
In capital letters to stress importance
Specific and positive, with reasons where useful
mcq.why: For example: “answer in under 80 words”.
distractors: Capitals are not a substitute for clarity.

mcq.q: What does prompt versioning involve?
options: Saving every prompt in the chat history of the session
Editing prompts directly in production when issues appear
Always switching to the newest model version on release
ID and version, review, evals, and the version logged per request
mcq.why: Treat prompts as code (18.1).
distractors: History is not versioned or reviewed.

mcq.q: A team keeps adding instructions without re-running the regression suite. What tends to happen?
options: Rules conflict and regressions go unnoticed
Nothing, as long as each rule is clear
Quality always rises with more rules
The prompt gets cheaper with each rule
mcq.why: Every change needs the evaluation set.

mcq.q: Where should the user's input go in a well-structured prompt?
options: First
Repeated in every section
In the system message
Last
mcq.why: Role, instructions, context, examples and format come before it.

mcq.q: A customer complains about one specific answer. What lets you trace exactly which instructions produced it?
options: The model's name alone, from the logs
The prompt version logged with the request
The prompt currently in the repository
The user's browser history for that day
mcq.why: The current prompt may have changed since then.
distractors: The prompt may have changed since.
The current prompt may differ from what ran.

mcq.q: A support prompt says “Do not mention competitors”, and the model keeps naming them when asked for comparisons. Which rewrite follows the topic's advice?
options: “Compare only our plans; if asked about others, say you can help with ours”
“NEVER, EVER mention competitors under any circumstances”
“Avoid anything that might be a problem for the business”
Remove the instruction and rely on the model's judgement
mcq.why: Specific, positive instructions with a clear alternative generalise better than bare prohibitions.
distractors: Capitals and repetition do not add clarity.
That gives no guidance at all.

covers: State that they are not instructions
Never rely on the prompt alone (16.2)

interview.q: {company}'s compliance team must approve every change to customer-facing prompts. Design the workflow.
covers: Prompts in the repository with IDs

interview.followUp: How would you roll back a bad prompt in minutes?

covers: Diverse examples across languages and trip types
interview.followUp: Relative dates like “next Friday” fail. How do you fix them?

mcq.q: What is context engineering?
options: Training a model on extra context
Writing the system prompt once at launch
Choosing the GPU that serves the model
Deciding which tokens go into each call
mcq.why: The window is a budget shared by instructions, tools, history, documents and output.
distractors: Context engineering changes inputs, not weights.

mcq.q: What happens when you include too much context?
options: The model simply ignores the extra material it does not need
Calls get slower and costlier, and the model is distracted
Answers always improve, because the model has more to go on
Nothing changes, apart from a few more tokens being used
mcq.why: Too little and it guesses; too much and quality and cost suffer.
distractors: It costs time, money and quality.

mcq.q: How do context assemblers usually prioritise?
options: Randomly, so that no source is ever favoured
Instructions and question first, then relevance
Alphabetically by the name of each source
Newest document first, and nothing else matters
mcq.why: Greedy inclusion by priority within the budget.

mcq.q: Which are compression techniques mentioned in the topic? Choose all that apply.
options: Summarising old turns
Removing duplicate chunks
Trimming documents to relevant passages
Deleting the system prompt
mcq.why: Replacing long tool outputs with extracted key fields is another.
distractors: The system prompt is always included.

mcq.q: Where should the most important material go in a long context?
options: Spread evenly through the context
It does not matter where it goes
Exactly in the middle of the context
Near the start or the end
mcq.why: Models attend less reliably to the middle of very long contexts.
distractors: Even spread puts much in the middle.
Position affects how reliably it is used.
The middle is used least reliably.

mcq.q: A recipe has system 900, tools 600, account facts 200, chunks 2,500, summary 300, last turns 800 tokens and an output reserve of 800. What is the total?
mcq.why: 5,300 tokens of input plus the 800-token output reserve.

mcq.q: That 6,100-token recipe runs in a 16,000-token window. Roughly what share of the window does it use?
options: About 38%
About 16%
About 61%
mcq.why: 6,100 ÷ 16,000 ≈ 38%, which is faster and cheaper than filling the window.
distractors: It leaves most of the window free.

mcq.q: Compression shortened a policy clause and the answer became wrong. What was likely lost?
options: Nothing important, only filler words
The output reserve for the answer
The tokenizer used by the model
An exception or effective date
mcq.why: Mark decision-critical text as never-summarise.
distractors: The answer changed, so something mattered.
The reserve is separate from the clause text.
Compression changes text, not the tokenizer.

mcq.q: Why must the budget include the output reserve?
options: Output is free, so it needs no space
Output shares the same window
The reserve is for logging the request
Providers require it by contract
mcq.why: Otherwise a long answer is cut off.
distractors: Output tokens use the window and cost money.
It is about how the window works.

mcq.q: In the assembler, you shrink the budget. What is dropped first?
options: The current question
The lowest-priority items
The system prompt
Everything equally
mcq.why: Always-included items stay; lower-priority ones go or get compressed.

interview.q: What is context engineering, and why does it matter?
covers: The model knows only its context
A budget shared by many sources
Too little: guessing; too much: cost and distraction
interview.followUp: Which source would you cut first when over budget?

covers: Middle of long contexts used less reliably
Important items near start or end

covers: Reranked chunks, dropped from the bottom

interview.q: How would you detect that context compression is losing critical details?
covers: Test cases that depend on exceptions and dates
Compare answers with and without compression

covers: Policy clauses with effective dates verbatim
interview.followUp: How would you check the summary kept every amount?

interview.followUp: How do you let each assistant tune its recipe safely?

interview.q: How would you measure whether a context recipe is good?
covers: Task success on an evaluation set
interview.followUp: Which ablation would you run first?

mcq.q: What is structured output?
options: Any text with clear headings and lists
A streamed response shown token by token
Data in a declared format, such as JSON Schema
A tool result returned to the model
mcq.why: It makes model output usable by code.
distractors: Formatting is not a machine-readable contract.

mcq.q: What does constrained decoding guarantee?
options: The output is factually correct
The output stays short
It parses against the schema
The model runs faster
mcq.why: It masks tokens that would break the schema; it guarantees shape, not truth.

mcq.q: The model returns valid JSON with the wrong refund amount. What was missing?
options: Streaming of the output
A higher temperature
A larger, stronger model
Checks against the source data
mcq.why: Validate values, not only shape.
distractors: Any model can err; code must check.

mcq.q: In tool calling, what does the model actually do?
options: It writes the function's code
It bypasses your application
It runs the function itself
It requests a call; your code decides
mcq.why: The model proposes; deterministic code disposes.
distractors: It requests calls to existing tools.

mcq.q: The model requests get_order(id="A-1043"). Who checks that this user may access that order?
options: Your code, using the authenticated session
Nobody, since order IDs are hard to guess
The tool's JSON schema, which checks the ID
The model, which knows the user from the chat
mcq.why: Never trust model-supplied IDs for authorisation (16.3).

mcq.q: What does streaming improve?
options: Time to first token
Answer accuracy
Total generation time
Token cost per answer
mcq.why: Both versions finish at the same time.
distractors: The full answer takes as long.

mcq.q: You stream JSON to the UI. When should your code act on it?
options: Before the model starts writing
Never, if the output is streamed
After validating the whole object
As soon as the first field arrives
mcq.why: Partial JSON may be incomplete or invalid.
distractors: There is nothing to act on yet.
Partial objects may change or be invalid.

mcq.q: How should large tool results be returned to the model?
options: In full, always
Trimmed, as a tool message
As a new system prompt
Hidden from the model
mcq.why: Large results waste context and can distract.
distractors: Tool results go in tool messages.
The model needs the result to answer.

mcq.q: Small local models make more tool-call mistakes. Why is that useful in a lab?
options: It is not useful for learning anything
They are wrong on every single call
You see the failures validation must handle
It proves large models are perfect
